transcript.text: I run an online shop in the UAE. I believe our revenue fell in the first quarter of 2026 against the last quarter of 2025, and my manager wants me to build a machine learning model that predicts revenue. I am the analyst; the result goes to the head of sales, who decides where to spend the next quarter's marketing money. The table I shared is our order export: one row per order, with its date, region, channel, product category, amount, status and customer. I do not know why revenue fell, or whether the export is complete for the latest months. [shares sales.csv]

[DCLab drew a chart with its numbers table and a chart with its numbers table and a chart with its numbers table above this message]

Here is what your order export actually says.

**Your belief is right, and the export looks complete.** It holds one row per order from 2025-01-01 to 2026-03-31 — the latest month runs to the 31st, so Q1 2026 is not a partial quarter. Counting only orders with status paid, revenue went from **87,551.17** (Oct–Dec 2025) to **72,682.06** (Jan–Mar 2026). Month by month (all order amounts): October **31,714.95**, November **33,463.4**, December **36,201.62**, then January **32,186.5**, February **26,344.62**, March **26,122.16**. And it is not just the post-December lull: March 2025 was **32,823.03** against March 2026's **26,122.16**.

**Three things need care before anyone builds a model.**

First, a model that predicts total revenue will not answer the question in front of your head of sales — where to put next quarter's money. Your export has no marketing spend, no traffic, no campaign, no price. A model can learn the shape of revenue over time; it cannot say which dirham of spend produced it. That gap is why I would do the diagnosis before the model, not instead of it.

Second, "revenue" needs a definition written down. In Q4 the export also holds **5,510.5** of cancelled orders (22) and **8,318.3** of refunded ones (40); in Q1, **3,271.95** cancelled (18) and **8,699.27** refunded (42). I read revenue as paid orders only and left the rest out — tell me if your finance view counts refunds differently.

Third, one warning if you do build: a model that uses `status` to predict revenue is cheating, because a refund or cancellation is only known after the order. And because refunds land late, today's Q1 paid figure may still fall as March orders get refunded.

**Where the money stopped** (charts and numbers above): paid revenue by channel was web **39,793.05 → 35,684.47** (165 orders → 158), app **33,698.98 → 22,368.95** (144 orders → 100), store **14,059.14 → 14,628.64** (62 → 60). The app is the bulk of the fall, and it lost orders, not basket size. By category (paid): home **24,202.23 → 16,182.34**, fashion **20,788.26 → 16,791.54**, beauty **21,795.88 → 18,236.3**, electronics **20,764.8 → 21,471.88** — home leads the drop, electronics held. By region (all order amounts): Dubai **40,730.82 → 33,882.27**, Abu Dhabi **24,783.32 → 21,318.59**, Sharjah **17,037.78 → 16,510.67**, Ajman **11,578.89 → 7,764**, Ras Al Khaimah **7,249.16 → 5,177.75**.

The plan:

1. Fix the definitions with you: revenue = paid orders only, Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 as the periods, refunds treated as they stand today. Checked by reconciling the status totals against the paid figures above.
2. Split each segment's fall into "fewer orders" versus "smaller baskets", and look at whether one region inside the app channel carries it. Checked by the segment falls adding back up to the total fall.
3. Test the seasonality claim like-for-like, comparing each 2026 month with the same month last year rather than with the previous quarter. Checked by both comparisons pointing the same way.
4. Then, and only then, the model the manager asked for: monthly paid revenue per channel and region, trained on earlier months, tested on the latest months it never saw. Checked by scoring it against a plain "same month last year" baseline and reporting both numbers.
5. Hand the head of sales one page: which segments lost what, the recommended direction for the budget, and plainly what this data cannot support.

Stop when: the head of sales has a named segment loss, a budget direction, and a forecast that either beats the naive baseline or is called out as not worth trusting.

If a step fails: if the segments do not add back to the total, I stop and tell you where the export disagrees with itself (most likely refund timing or an order appearing twice); if the model cannot beat "same month last year", I will say the model is not justified by this data rather than hand over a number that looks precise, and tell you what to collect next.

The three options above cover it: the diagnosis is what I would do first, the model second, and the dashboard as the thing you keep. Which one do you want me to start?

transcript.text: I lead retention at a subscription company. I want a model that tells us, for each customer, which discount to offer (none, 10 percent or 25 percent) so that they do not leave. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. We have never given discounts before, so there is no record of any offer or of how customers reacted. The retention team would use the result every month. [shares customers.csv]

Understood: you want each customer assigned the smallest discount that keeps them, reviewed monthly by your team.

**The problem as it really is.** Your table can tell you who is likely to leave — of 1,200 customers, 17.4% churned the next month, 22.4% on basic plans against 14.5% premium and 11.1% plus, and it rises with support tickets (15.5% at zero tickets, 24.5% at three). What it cannot tell you is what a discount does. You've never given one, so all 1,200 rows are customers who were offered nothing: there is no variation in the treatment and no recorded reaction to it. A model that claims to pick between 10 and 25 percent from this file would not be learning anything about discounts — it would be inventing the effect and dressing it up as a prediction.

**Two things to care about before any work.** First, who is *at risk* and who is *persuadable* are different people. Your highest-risk customers are often the ones leaving for reasons a discount cannot touch, and your low-risk ones would stay anyway — spending on them is waste. Only data from actual offers can separate those groups, which is exactly what you don't have yet. Second, please don't target discounts on city: it's a stand-in for who your customers are rather than what they did, it has no bearing on churn you can defend, and charging different effective prices by geography is the kind of thing regulators and your own customers notice. Plan and segment as eligibility rules are fine; city as a lever is not.

**The ways this could go.** (a) A churn-risk score today: usable next month, honest about what it knows, but silent on which discount. (b) A randomized discount test: the only route that can eventually answer your actual question, at the cost of a few months and a deliberate spend on customers who might not have been offered anything. (c) Reporting on current churn drivers: cheapest, fastest, but no per-customer action. I'd do (a) now *as the input to* (b), because your risk score is what makes a clean test — randomize offers within risk bands and you learn far more per customer you pay for.

The plan

1. Build a churn-risk model on your 1,200 customers, predicting churned_next_month from signup date, tenure, plan, segment, monthly spend and support tickets, with city excluded as a targeting input. Checked by time-split validation (train on earlier signups, test on later ones) so the score reflects how it will actually be used, not a lucky shuffle.
2. Score every current customer and show you the risk bands with counts, so you can see how many people each band holds before anyone promises discounts.
3. Design the discount test: 10 percent, 25 percent and a control group, randomized inside risk bands, with the sample size each arm needs, the metric (churn within the month after the offer) and how long to run before reading it. Checked against your budget and eligibility rules, which I still need from you.
4. Run the first month of the test, record each offer and each outcome, and add that to the table.
5. Once the arms hold enough customers, train the uplift/policy model that picks a discount per customer, and validate it by comparing discounted and non-discounted customers in the same risk band. Checked by holding out one month.
6. Hand the retention team a monthly refresh: risk score, then recommended offer, with the share of customers in each recommendation tracked.

Stop when you have a working risk score and a test design your team can launch, and no discount number is claimed anywhere before step 5 shows real offer data.
If a step fails: if validation shows the risk model barely beats the 17.4% base rate, we report the drivers plainly instead of a score, and the test still goes ahead — it doesn't depend on the model.

The three choices above are the same route cut into pieces: I'd take the first now and the second right after it, since the risk bands from the model are what make the test statistically clean. The dashboard is useful for the team but doesn't move you toward discount answers, so I'd hold it until the pilot is live.

transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a travel agency. I want to predict, at the moment a booking is made, whether it will be cancelled, so the operations team can overbook the right trips. The table I shared is our bookings up to late February 2026: booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. Some of the trips in it have not happened yet. Operations would score every new booking once, on the day it is made. [shares bookings.csv]

Here's what I took from your brief and from the table itself.

**The problem as I understand it.** You want a score, produced the moment a booking is written, that says how likely that booking is to be cancelled — so operations can decide how many extra places to sell on each departure. The customer is the operations team, and the hard constraint is timing: only what is known on the booking day can be in the model. Your table has 1,500 bookings, booked 2025-01-01 through 2026-02-24, travelling as late as 2026-08-16, across 865 distinct customers.

**Three things that need care before any modelling.**

- *Immature labels.* 1,176 rows are trips that have already ended; their cancellation flag is final and they cancel at 22.1%. The other 324 rows are future trips — 25.6% of them already show cancelled = 1, and the rest can still flip, so treating their zeros as "did not cancel" teaches the model a rate that is too low. Those 324 belong in scoring, not in training as negatives. The price to pay for the clean version is a smaller training set; the price to pay for the big one is a biased model.
- *Repeat customers.* 1,500 bookings over 865 customer_ids means the same traveller appears several times. A random split lets the model meet the same person in the holdout and overstates its accuracy. The split has to be by booking date and hold customers whole.
- *The overbooking decision itself.* The table carries no seat capacity, no cancellation date and no no-show flag, so no model here can say how many places to sell. It can only give a per-booking probability that operations sum per trip and compare with capacity. And one feature is worth a deliberate choice rather than a default: nationality is known at booking time, but it feeds a decision that can end up refusing a traveller a place — that is usually better left out, or at least tested for how much it actually adds.

**How I'd start.** Not with the model: with the maturity audit and a baseline. I checked the obvious segments already — destination runs 18.9% (Paris) to 26.2% (Dubai); web bookings with free cancellation sit at 25.2% against 20.3% for app bookings without it; monthly rates stay in a 19.5%–27.8% band with no trend to chase. That gives the lift a model has to beat, stated as numbers before anyone trains anything.

So, the two ways to begin, your pick in spirit but I recommend the first: **start with the preparation-and-baseline step** (drop the 12 TEST rows, restrict to the 1,176 mature bookings, build the date-based split with customers held whole, and report cancellation rates by lead-time band, destination, channel and free-cancellation flag), then build the model on top of it; or go **straight to the model** and let the split handle the maturity implicitly, which is faster but hides the 324-row bias inside a single accuracy figure.

One question that changes the plan most: **how long before the travel date can a booking still be cancelled** — is it the free-cancellation window, or a paid policy cutoff? Tell me that and I'll set the label horizon, and I'll assume 2026-02-24 as the maturity line unless your policy says otherwise.
